chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 181 to 200: short poems mostly in the wife's voice waiting through the rains (the mullai budding, evening, thunder, the cold season as Death), with a threatened palm horse, a fisher girl's net of eyes, a husband's turned taste for the wife at home, and a lover who promises his pain will outlast this life.

181.reading: The wife asks her friend what good there is in the harsh word 'that is how she is', spoken in the quarrel, against women like them who have grown old as matrons carrying the many duties of the great house of the man from a town where a newly calved buffalo grazes the green crop near the calf the ploughman has tied, never moving away from it.
181.nuance: She calls herself and her kind பெருமுது பெண்டிர், the old matrons who bear the house's many burdens, so the sting of the word is that it is said to a wife whose years of service should have earned better. The mother buffalo that will not leave its tied calf is read by some as the hero kept near home by his son while he grazes elsewhere; only one correspondence (staying near the child) can be made firm, so it fails the two-pair condition and stays scene. Who spoke the harsh word (the hero, or someone of the parathai's side) is not said.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the ploughman and the crop field belong to the watered fields

182.reading: The lover asks whether it will bring her to him if he ties a great garland hung with bells to the palm-stem horse cut from a fine-crowned palmyra, wears white bones, shows himself so that others mock, throws off his great shame for one day and goes down the street, since the simple girl of the swaying gait has not softened to the messenger they sent.
182.nuance: The verb is a question (தருவது கொல்லோ): he weighs the madal as a last resort and counts its cost in the mockery of others before he has mounted it. The contrast ஒருநாள் / பெருநாண் sets one day's display against a lifetime's shame.

thinai_evidence.note: a threatened, not yet ridden, palm horse after a failed message keeps the poem inside the courtship

183.reading: The wife wonders whether, in the land he went to, where the fresh konrai blossoms turn pale as she does, her man will see the stag with twisted horns parted like himself from its small-headed doe, there in the poor forest tract where the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck.
183.nuance: Two similes run in opposite directions: the flower is like her (நம்போல்), the stag is like him (தம்போல்). The season marks both partners, and her hope is that the sight of a parted pair will teach him what she feels. The stag is the subject of her question, so striking it removes the poem's sense; it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: forest scrub and the konrai's bloom set the land and the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the konrai blossoms that yellow as her skin pales

comparisons.vehicle: தம்போற் சிறுதலைப் பிணையிற் றீர்ந்த நெறிகோட் டிரலை
comparisons.tenor: the absent man, parted from her as the stag from its doe
the dark-blue kaayaa blossoms on the branch

184.reading: The lover tells his companions that the wise do not bear false witness and warns them off the little fishing village: his noble heart, not weighing what is fit for what, fell there and is lost in the seaside grove where the young daughter of fishermen with fine nets, a doll with a fine knot of hair like a peacock's eye, catches men in the net of her eyes.
184.nuance: The fishermen's fine net (நுண்வலை) and the daughter's net of eyes (கண்வலை) stand in successive lines: the girl practises her family's trade on men. The opening maxim is his reply to a companion's rebuke: he claims the evidence of his own lost heart as testimony the wise cannot doubt.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen and their nets belong to the shore

comparisons.tenor: the girl's fine knot of hair
the fisher girl
her eyes that catch his heart as her father's net catches fish

185.reading: The girl asks her friend what would come of telling the man of the land where the bright red kaanthal, closed like a striped snake that has let down its hood, ruined by the east wind, droops over the rock, that she has become like this through him: her brow pale, her spots faded, her long soft shoulders thinned, her bangles slipping, and her fine dark body in a state of ruinous grief.
185.nuance: The kaanthal beaten down by the wind and hanging over the rock is the traditional figure of her own ruined beauty and, some say, of the man as hard as the rock it hangs on; only one firm pair (flower to her beauty) can be named, so it is not tagged ullurai. Her question is a refusal: she will not use her wasting as a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal on the rock of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the kaanthal flower folding shut after the storm

186.reading: The girl tells her friend that for the man of the land where the soft mullai creeper of the forest field, wedded by the rains with their loud thunder, has put out buds like teeth, her eyes have given up sleep.
186.nuance: The rains 'wed' the land (மணந்த), and the creeper buds like a row of teeth, as if the season smiles at her: union and laughter in the land, sleeplessness in her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the first rains on the forest field

comparisons.tenor: the mullai buds, white and pointed like teeth

187.reading: The girl tells her friend that the man of the land where the kid of the mountain goat, bedded on red rock, drinks its fill of the sweet milk pouring from the udder and leaps in the shade of the great hill is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts.
187.nuance: Kapilar sets வலியன் against மெலியும்: the man is hard as stone, her heart grows soft, and the same root (வலி) is turned three ways in two lines. The kid nursed full and sheltered in the hill's shade is the care his own land gives its young and he withholds from her.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain goat and the great hill

comparisons.tenor: the man's hardness of heart

iraicchi.act: the kid is fed to the full from its mother's udder and plays safe in the shade of the hill
iraicchi.sense: in his land even the young of beasts are nourished and sheltered, yet he leaves her uncared for

188.reading: The wife says the mullai buds have ripened, and with the mullai the wide field of the cool rains has come to its beauty; the man who loosened her bright bangles has not come, and evening has come, aiming at her fine beauty.
188.nuance: The verb முற்றின is repeated for the buds and for the field's beauty, and then answered by வாரார் and வந்தன்று: the land has come to fullness on time, he has not come, and evening has come in his place.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool rains, the field and evening

comparisons.tenor: evening as an enemy coming against her beauty

189.reading: The man says the errand is one of going today and coming back tomorrow: his white chariot will race like a waterfall coming down the hill, its bright wheel like the young crescent cutting the green crop like a firebrand falling from the sky, and travelling like the wind it will reach her by evening, and he will embrace the many-graced body of the young girl with few rows of white bangles and be glad.
189.nuance: The addressee is not named; the chariot images suggest the charioteer. All the poem's speed belongs to the return: the parting is reduced to one day by the man, and the speed of the images measures his longing. Whether he speaks before setting out (a short parting, paalai) or on the road home (mullai) is open, as the colophon variants show.

thinai_evidence.note: a man setting out on a short journey, reckoning his return

comparisons.tenor: the white chariot racing
the bright wheel
the wheel slicing the crop
the chariot's speed

190.reading: The wife asks her friend whether the man who stroked her dark curled hair and great shoulders and left to make wealth, loosening her close bangles, knows of the single bell of the stall of many cows that rings each time the good bull moves, at the midnight of half-darkness when the mighty thunder roars to sever the green head of the angry spotted snake.
190.nuance: That she hears the bull's one bell at every step is the proof that she lies awake; the thunder that kills the snake is the night's terror, the small bell its loneliness. His parting caress (நீவி) is remembered as the act that loosened her bangles.

thinai_evidence.note: the herders' cattle stall in the rains at midnight

191.reading: The wife says, look there, what shall I call this: a flock of dark-winged birds perched on a strong branch, having paired, call in sweet voices into the hearts of the parted; hearing them, she would have said to the stranger who left, should he come here, 'do not dress my thick hair with flowers, do not touch me', if only she could.
191.nuance: மன்னே marks the resolve as one she knows she will not keep: she rehearses refusing his touch and his flowers, and the particle concedes she will yield. ஏதிலாளர், 'strangers', is her word for her own husband.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for one who has gone, in the season of mating birds

iraicchi.act: the birds pair and stay together on the branch, calling
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep with their mates in this season, while he has gone off like a stranger

192.reading: Told 'he will come right here, do not grieve', the wife asks whether she should not weep now, she who lives wasting with this pain, when the dark koel with glossy feathers, like a touchstone streaked bright with gold, tears at the fragrant pollen on the mango branch, and at this hour she strokes her hair empty of flowers.
192.nuance: வறுங்குரல் கூந்தல், hair empty of flowers, says without saying it that she has not dressed her hair since he left; stroking it is all the touch it gets. The touchstone simile turns the koel into the assayer of the season: gold on black, the proof that spring has come.

thinai_evidence.note: the koel in the mango blossom marks the spring of parting

comparisons.tenor: the black koel dusted with yellow pollen

193.reading: The girl says the man of the land where the open-mouthed frog in the narrow-mouthed pool, like a gem-bowl filled with toddy, croaks like a clapper drum, embraced her long shoulders in the long white moonlight of last month; today the mullai buds are fragrant.
193.nuance: The poem's whole lament is in the two time-words: தொல்லைத் திங்கள், last month's moon, when he held her, and இன்று, today, when only the mullai is fragrant. The tattai is the clapper used to scare birds from the millet, so the frog's croak is a sound of the hill fields she remembers him by.

thinai_evidence.note: the passing of a month and the mullai's bloom set a time of waiting

comparisons.tenor: the small rock pool
the frog's croaking

194.reading: The girl asks her friend what this can be called: the sky roars with lightning flashing, that is one thing; against it the forest peacock cries out fiercely; for these two strangers that have joined together, her foolish heart is thrown into great turmoil.
194.nuance: ஏதில, 'things that are nothing to me': the cloud and the peacock answer each other, a pair that has met while she has not, and her heart is shaken by a union that has no business with her. The peacock answers the thunder, so the bird is the subject of the poem, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: lightning and rain-thunder over the forest

195.reading: The wife asks where they are now, the men gone to finish the work they wanted, as the sun, its anger cooled, reaches the hill in the sorrowful evening that rises bearing grief; alas, they do not say 'she suffers, she laments', not knowing that her body, like a crafted doll through which the caressing, swaying wind passes, has become something else.
195.nuance: The wind is caressing (தைவரல்) where he is not, and her body has become an object it plays over. The plural verbs make her charge general: the men who go for their work do not say the words that would show they know.

thinai_evidence.note: sunset and the grief of evening

comparisons.tenor: her body, lifeless and changed

196.reading: The friend tells the husband that once, when her friend gave him the green fruit of the neem, he called it a lump of sweet jaggery, and now, when she gives him the cool clear water of the cold spring on Pari's Parambu in the month of Thai, he says it is hot and brackish; such, sir, is the way of love.
196.nuance: The irony is in the last line: அற்றால் அன்பின் பாலே presents his fickleness as a law of love itself. Nothing she gives has changed; what he tastes has, and the friend's two examples make the bitter sweet and the sweetest bitter.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's love that has turned, reproached by the friend

197.reading: The wife asks her friend what they can do: painfully, Death in the shape of the cold season, with clustered rain-clouds that have drawn up the sea's water and gathered, confused and wild with the cold north wind, is coming, aimed at her who is parted from her lover.
197.nuance: Season and Death are fused in one phrase, கூதிர் உருவில் கூற்றம், Death wearing the cold season as its body, and it aims at her alone (எற் குறித்து), as evening aims at the wife's beauty in 188.

thinai_evidence.note: a parted wife's helpless lament

comparisons.tenor: the cold season, seen as Death come for her

198.reading: The friend tells the man with a chest fragrant with sandal from the forest of Malaiyan, whose great hand shines with the spear of killing war, that they are going to drive off the parrots settling on the red millet sown where the yaa trees were felled and burned, millet with green stems and bases like sugarcane and dense green ears, dripping milk like the trunk of a young cow-elephant and bowed on their dark stalks; he should not come here, for her mother is coming.
198.nuance: The refusal carries an invitation: telling him where they are going (to the millet field to scare parrots) while forbidding him the house names the place he may meet her. Malaiyan's war epithet is spent on a forest that perfumes the lover's chest.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the millet's thick base
the drooping millet ear

199.reading: The lover tells his heart that even if it does not come to winning her, one thing is sure: this love-sickness for the dark woman with curled, oiled hair fragrant with the wind that touches the forest of Ori of the strong chariots and generous hand will, with a closeness like today's, have no end and will last on in the other world.
199.nuance: He takes comfort not in winning her but in the endlessness of the pain: the illness (நோய்) itself is promised continuance in the next world, a consolation turned into a vow.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's longing in courtship, unsure of winning her

comparisons.tenor: the bond continuing as it is today

200.reading: The wife tells her friend that even the cool, flower-scented torrent that comes down from the hill where rain has fallen, carrying flowers strewn on the heights, has come, but he has not; surely he has forgotten, though she does not forget; the dark evening clouds of the season's rain rumble with their sweet-voiced thunder, the season before which he promised to come back when he left.
200.nuance: The -உம் of புனலும் ('even the torrent') makes the flood a rival traveller: water from the hills keeps its time and arrives, he does not. மறந்தோர் மன்ற மறவா நாமே balances the two verbs of forgetting in five words.

thinai_evidence.note: the seasonal rains at evening

links.note: Kuruntokai 182: the lover asks whether throwing off his great shame (பெருநாண் நீக்கி) and riding the palm horse through the street will win her after the messenger failed; Kural 1132: body and life will mount the palm horse once shame is put aside (நாணினை நீக்கி).
links.teaches: The Kural states the madal threat as a general law of the unbearable, while the Kuruntokai shows its occasion (a failed go-between) and counts its price in other men's mockery, so the Kural's 'putting shame aside' is a public cost the hero weighs, not a private loss.

links.note: Kuruntokai 184: the hero tells his companions his heart is caught in the net of the fisher girl's eyes; Kural 1084: the man says the artless girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them.
links.teaches: Both men describe a first sight as the girl's eyes acting on them, but the Kuruntokai draws the weapon from her own people's trade (the fishermen's fine net), showing that the Kural's abstract killing gaze was, in the older poetry, given a landscape and a craft.

links.note: Kuruntokai 185: the girl asks what use it is to tell him she has wasted because of him; Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts her is hearing him called cruel.
links.teaches: Both heroines decline to blame the man for their wasting body, but for opposite reasons: the Kural's woman defends him, the Kuruntokai's expects no answer from a man as unmoved as the rock under the beaten kaanthal, so the same refusal can be loyalty or despair.

links.note: Kuruntokai 187: he is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts; Kural 1291: she asks her heart why it is not hers when his heart stays with him.
links.teaches: Kapilar gives the image and the Kural the argument of one complaint: the man's heart keeps to itself like stone while hers goes over to him, and together they show the heroine's quarrel is with her own heart's softness more than with his hardness.

links.note: Kuruntokai 188: evening has come, aiming at her beauty, when the mullai has budded and he has not come; Kural 1221: she tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the lives of wives.
links.teaches: The Kuruntokai shows why the evening attacks: it arrives with the season he promised to return by, so its hostility is the broken promise made visible, which the Kural's address to the evening leaves unstated.

links.note: Kuruntokai 190: at midnight in the storm she hears the cattle stall's one bell ring with every step of the bull; Kural 1168: the night that puts all beings to sleep has her alone for company.
links.teaches: The Kural's claim that she alone keeps the night company is proved in the Kuruntokai by what she hears: only a wakeful listener counts the bull's every step by its bell, so the single sound measures the sleepless solitude the couplet asserts.

links.note: Kuruntokai 192 and Akananuru 97: the friend says do not grieve (இனையல், ஆழேல்), and the heroine answers that she cannot stop weeping when the koel calls in the flowering mango.
links.teaches: The same reply to the same comfort shows the spring koel in the mango was a fixed answer in the heroine's mouth: the long Akananuru spends its lines on the dangers of his road, while the Kuruntokai replaces them with the gesture of stroking flowerless hair, so the short form puts the proof in her body rather than in the landscape.

links.note: Kuruntokai 196: the husband who once called neem sweet now calls the cool spring water of Pari's Parambu hot and brackish; Purananuru 176: the poet regrets the days lost like people who scorned the clear spring of Parambu because it was in their own town.
links.teaches: Read with the Purananuru, the friend's choice of Parambu's water carries its proverbial lesson: the sweetest thing is scorned when it is near, so she diagnoses the husband's turning as contempt bred by having the wife at home.

links.note: Kuruntokai 199: the lover tells his heart his love-sickness will last on into the other world; Kural 1315: he told her they would not part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
links.teaches: The Kural's joke works only because Paranar's belief was the convention: love was expected to outlast this birth, so a lover who promised only 'this birth' had set a limit the older poem's lover would not accept.

links.note: Kuruntokai 200: surely he has forgotten, but we do not forget; Kural 1207: what would become of her if she forgot, when she knows no forgetting and remembering burns.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps forgetting inside the woman, as a danger she cannot afford, while Avvaiyar turns it outward as a charge against the man, proven by the rains that came on time, so the same refusal to forget can be self-torment or an accusation.

links.note: Kuruntokai 183: the wife wonders whether he will see the stag parted from its doe; Akananuru 34: the hero, seeing a stag feed and guard its doe, bids his chariot hurry home.
links.teaches: The pair shows the stag and doe of the scrub working from both ends of a separation: the waiting wife hopes he will see a parted pair and feel her loss, while the returning hero is moved by a pair together, so the same creatures carry absence for her and return for him.

source_issues: kuruntokai:182 line 6: our text reads கலிந்தவிர்; tamilvu.org has கலிழ் கவின், sangamtamil.com கலிழ்ந்து அவிர் (flag). The word qualifies her gait and does not change the poem's sense.
kuruntokai:183 line 3: repaired from tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), agreeing with sangamtamil.com (flag).
kuruntokai:189: colophon thinai பாலை in the base text, முல்லை in sangamtamil.com (flag); the poem can be read as a man setting out (paalai) or returning (mullai). Base kept; marked uncertain.
kuruntokai:194 line 2: வானோர் பிரங்கும் is hard to divide (வான் ஓர்பு இரங்கும?); read as the sky roaring. Marked uncertain.
kuruntokai:198 lines 6-7: கானத் / தார is ஆரம் (sandal) split across the line break; the karu form is given as written on line 7.
